Where it began

Mitchell Johnson was born in Townsville, Queensland, on 2 November 1981. His first sporting love was tennis, and his hero was Pete Sampras. At 14 he turned down the chance to move to Brisbane to chase a tennis career, and only at 17 did he put the racket aside for cricket.

He was noticed quickly. At a fast bowling clinic in Brisbane that same year, Dennis Lillee picked him out and got in touch with his old team-mate Rod Marsh, and the teenager was soon at the national academy in Adelaide. He toured England with the Under-19 side in 1999, then began his first-class career with Queensland. The first ball he ever faced in first-class cricket, against New Zealand, he hit for six.

The player

His first Test came at the Gabba in November 2007, against Sri Lanka. In all he played 73 Tests between 2007 and 2015, taking 313 wickets at 28.41, with 12 five-wicket innings and three ten-wicket matches. He also made 2,065 runs, with a hundred and 11 fifties.

The great days came in bursts. At Perth in December 2008 he took seven South African wickets for 12 in a single day's play on his way to 8 for 61. In South Africa early in 2009 he struck 96 not out and then a first Test hundred, 123 not out, reached in just 86 balls. Best of all was the 2013–14 Ashes at home, after a year out of the side. He took 37 wickets as Australia won all five Tests, and was man of the series. He followed it with 22 wickets in South Africa, including 12 for 127 at Centurion.

What made him special

Pace, above all, and plenty of it. He was the quickest bowler, by calendar, to reach 150 Test wickets, needing just 2 years and 139 days. He was also a dangerous left-handed hitter down the order, and in 2009 became the first Australian to make 300 runs and take 30 wickets in a calendar year.

When the rhythm deserted him, the ball could wander rather freely. When it clicked he was a handful, and his comebacks were the making of him.

Away from the middle

He won the Sir Garfield Sobers Trophy as ICC Cricketer of the Year twice, in 2009 and 2014, the second year adding ICC Test Player of the Year and the Allan Border Medal. He left international cricket in November 2015 at the WACA, his adopted home ground, where the New Zealand players formed a guard of honour as he walked out to bat. A spell with the Perth Scorchers followed, including 3 for 3 in four overs, before he finished with all cricket in 2018. His autobiography, Resilient, came out in 2016, and in 2020 he took part in the television series SAS Australia.

And finally

For a man who did everything on the field with his left hand, he writes with his right. Tennis lost a player and cricket gained one, though England's batsmen of 2013–14 might have voted the other way.
